slides.title: 800 years ago, a boy got bored doing his homework.

slides.body:
For everyday writing, people here didn't use costly parchment. They scratched words into soft birch bark with a pointed tool of metal or bone.

Letters, business deals, shopping lists, even a marriage proposal.

slides.kicker: Some of it was a child's homework.
slides.body:
Around the mid-1200s, a boy of about six or seven practised his alphabet, repeated syllables and copied lines from the Psalms.

Then, in the margins, he started to draw.
His figures have anywhere from three to eight fingers. He probably hadn't learned to count yet.

On one piece he drew a creature with a long neck, pointed ears and a curly tail, and labelled it as himself.

On another: “Greetings from Onfim to Danilo.” Most likely a classmate.

Novgorod's wet, oxygen-poor soil preserved the bark for centuries. Since 1951, archaeologists have dug up more than a thousand birch-bark texts there.

Seventeen of them are Onfim's.

slides.kicker: No chronicle bothered to record this.
slides.body:
Official history tells us about princes and wars. Onfim's scraps show something nobody thought worth writing down.

How a child learned to read, 800 years ago. And how his mind wandered.

slides.lead: History remembers what people meant to leave behind.
slides.accent: But it often learns the most from what they never meant to keep.

slides.line: Save this for the next time you doodle in a meeting.

caption:
Around 800 years ago, a boy in Novgorod was supposed to be practising his alphabet on strips of birch bark. Instead, he drew knights, horses and himself as a wild beast.

The mud kept it all, and today his homework is one of the most charming windows into medieval childhood. ✏️

What would future historians learn from your doodles?
